title: The City Even the Wind Could Not Enter
story:
Somewhere beyond the seven continents lay a city so perfectly sealed that not even the wind could pass through its gates without the king's consent — and the only man who could walk into it freely was an actor.

The city of Vajra belonged to the Asura king Vajranabha, and he had won it the hard way. On the summit of Mount Sumeru he had stood in long austerities until Brahma himself appeared and offered him a boon. The demon asked for two things: that no god should ever be able to kill him, and that he should possess the city of Vajra — a city where even the air could not easily enter, ringed with gardens and dependent towns, rich in peerless jewels, a city that granted every wish before the wish was even spoken. Brahma said yes to both.

Millions of Asuras took refuge with their new king. Enemies of the gods, they lived in Vajra's gardens and branch cities healthy, well-fed, and content, safe under the shelter of the boon. Elated by his good fortune, Vajranabha began to think of ruling everything. He went to Indra, king of the gods, and announced that the three worlds belonged to all the sons of the sage Kashyapa alike — he wished to govern them, and if Indra did not approve, he could give battle.

Indra consulted Brihaspati, and the two of them chose to wait: their father Kashyapa was in the middle of a great sacrifice, and when it ended, he would do what was fair. Vajranabha carried the same answer to Kashyapa himself, who sent him home with the same promise, and the Asura returned to his city to bide his time.

But Indra did not sit idle. He came secretly to Dwaraka and told Krishna everything. Krishna's answer was calm: the horse-sacrifice of Vasudeva, his father, was at hand; once it was over, he would kill Vajranabha. He was also honest about the difficulty. "Even the wind cannot enter his city," he said, "if Vajranabha does not wish it. At the right hour we will find a way in."

The way in came during the sacrifice itself. An actor named Bhadra so delighted the great saints assembled for the horse-sacrifice that they invited him to ask for a boon. Prompted by Krishna, and as if urged on by the goddess of learning herself, Bhadra asked: that he might roam freely over the seven continents of the earth and through the sky, with nothing to obstruct him; that he might be strong and unharmed by any creature, moving or still; that he might take whatever form he pleased; that age might never touch him; and that the sages might always be pleased with him. "So be it," the Munis said.

From that day the immortal-looking actor ranged over the whole earth. He performed in the cities of the Danava kings, in Uttarakuru, Bhadrashva, Ketumala, and the island of Kalamra, and on every festival day he came back to Dwaraka, where the Yadavas welcomed him.

Then Indra called the Dhartarashtra swans — celestial birds, and his own brothers, since both gods and swans are begotten by Kashyapa. "The great duty of killing the enemies of the gods awaits us," he told them, "and you must help. Keep this counsel secret. You may go anywhere you like, so go to the city of Vajra, where no one else can enter, and swim in the tanks of the king's inner palace. Vajranabha has a daughter, Prabhavati, fair as moonlight, the jewel of the three worlds, kept by her friends for a swayamvara. Describe to her the family, beauty, character, and accomplishments of the high-souled Pradyumna until her heart is won; then carry her words to Pradyumna and bring back his. Report to me and to my younger brother Krishna at Dwaraka every day. The Danavas cannot be slain by the gods — Brahma's boon protects them. Their destruction must come from the sons of the gods, from Pradyumna and his brothers. And the door of the sealed city will open through Bhadra's boon, for the Yadavas will enter in the guise of his troupe."

So the swans rose into the sky and turned toward a city no army could approach, carrying in their breasts a message that would open it from within — not through any breach in its walls, but through the heart of the king's own daughter.
reflection: Krishna's strategy is characteristic: against a fortress that no power can breach, he sends not an army but an actor and a song. The impenetrable city is entered by art — and by the love of the one person inside it whom no wall was meant to keep out.
next_story_tease: Before long the swans would be swimming in Vajranabha's own pleasure-tanks — and a troupe of actors would be on the road to his city.
hero_scene: At Vasudeva's horse-sacrifice, the actor Bhadra stands before the assembled sages with arms raised in salute as his boon is granted, while high above, unseen by any mortal, Indra's white swans bank toward the distant towers of the sealed city of Vajra.
